extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining claim construction and the written description requirement under 35 U.S.C. §112 (including para. 6 means-plus-function), explaining how to assess whether the specification shows possession of the claimed invention and how to interpret claim language (preambles, transitional phrases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — interpret each claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers; give each claim its broadest reasonable interpretation in light of and consistent with the written description. Consider the entire claim including preamble language and the transitional phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate preamble language and whether it constitutes a structural limitation by reviewing the entire application. Apply the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification. Do not import limitations from the specification into the claims. Give weight to preamble language where the claim as a whole suggests it; resolve preamble importation by considering what the inventors actually invented and intended to encompass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of transitional terms (comprising / consisting essentially of / consisting of)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize differences among transitional phrases: 'comprising' is open-ended, 'consisting of' is closed, and 'consisting essentially of' is a middle ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'comprising' as covering the recited elements alone or with unrecited elements. Treat 'consisting essentially of' as open to unlisted ingredients that do not materially affect the basic and novel properties of the invention; absent clear specification of what those basic/novel characteristics are, 'consisting essentially of' will be construed as equivalent to 'comprising' for prior art (35 U.S.C. 102/103) purposes. If applicant contends that additional steps/materials are excluded by 'consisting essentially of,' the applicant bears the burden of showing that such additions would materially change the invention's characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the entire application for support of each element/step
rubrics_metrics.description: Before deciding whether the disclosure satisfies the written description requirement, review the claims and the entire specification—including embodiments, figures, and sequence listings—to understand how applicant provides support for the features of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the field of the invention and the level of skill in the art; there is generally an inverse correlation between level of skill and the specificity of disclosure required. Information well known in the art need not be described in detail. Use patents and printed publications in the art to assess whether the art is mature and what disclosure is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to show possession of the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession may be shown by describing an actual reduction to practice, by clear depiction in detailed drawings or structural chemical formulas, or by disclosure of sufficiently detailed identifying characteristics that a skilled artisan would recognize applicant had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: construction of an embodiment or performance of a process meeting all claim limitations (reduction to practice); detailed drawings/structural formulas; deposits for biological materials per 37 CFR 1.801 et seq.; identifying characteristics such as sequence, structure, binding affinity/specificity, molecular weight, length, restriction maps, expression data. The description need only detail what is new or nonconventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of functional descriptions (function vs structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition by function alone generally does not suffice to describe certain inventions (e.g., coding sequences); adequacy may require precise definitions such as structure, formula, chemical name, or physical properties rather than mere function or a plan to obtain the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function plus a known correlation to structure may suffice where the art supports predicting structure from function; function alone is little more than a wish and will not satisfy written description absent such correlation. Assess whether one skilled in the art could determine the structure from the disclosed function with reasonable confidence. For software/microprocessor arts, disclosure of a capable microprocessor may be sufficient when one skilled in the art would know how to program it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. §112, sixth paragraph) support and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. §112, para. 6, it must be interpreted to cover the corresponding structure, materials, or acts in the specification and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine adequacy by: (1) whether the written description adequately links particular structure/materials/acts to the recited function; or (2) whether one skilled in the art would have known what structure/materials/acts perform the recited function based on the application (including original claims, abstract, drawings). A rejection under §112, para. 2 cannot stand where §112, first paragraph provides adequate description for means-plus-function recitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drawn to a single embodiment/species — stepwise written description analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim drawn to a single embodiment or species, determine whether the application (A) describes an actual reduction to practice; (B) if not, whether there is reduction to drawings or structural chemical formulas sufficiently detailed; (C) if not, whether distinguishing identifying characteristics are set forth that show possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically: (1) If the application describes the complete structure (or acts of a process) of the claimed invention as a whole, the written description requirement is satisfied. (2) If not, determine whether other identifying characteristics are disclosed in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms that a skilled artisan would recognize possession. Consider established correlations between structure and function; where present, function plus minimal structure may suffice; where absent, function alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in assessing written description possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the specification shows possession is a factual determination based on multiple factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include: level of skill and knowledge in the art; disclosure of partial structure; physical and/or chemical properties; functional characteristics coupled with a known/disclosed correlation between function and structure; and the method of making the claimed invention. Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one skilled in the art to conclude applicant was in possession is sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varying disclosure requirements by technology maturity and predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: The description needed to satisfy §112, first paragraph varies with the nature and scope of the invention and with existing scientific and technological knowledge; mature predictable arts require less detailed disclosure than emerging, unpredictable technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mature fields where knowledge/skill is high, a written description objection should generally not be raised for claims present in the original filing even if the specification only discloses a method and its function. In unpredictable/emerging technologies, more evidence (e.g., reduction to practice, detailed structure) is required. For product-by-process claims, the written description is satisfied where the process has actually been used to produce the product; otherwise disclosure of process alone may not support a product claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of definitions for well-established terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of definitions or details for well-established terms or procedures should not be the basis for a rejection under 35 U.S.C. §112, first paragraph, for lack of adequate written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require restatement of conventional, well-known information in the specification. Rely on the common knowledge of one skilled in the art when appropriate.
